Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

The pump gauge still showed its usual range, so she checked the filter and the main valve before opening the repair area. The filter screen held a small amount of leaf grit but was not blocked. The valve handle moved freely, and there was no visible leak around its fittings. She recorded the pressure readings and marked the wet ground with two orange flags so the crew could return to the same location after the soil dried.

The affected lateral runs about 110 meters along the lower side of the block. It serves 24 young pear trees and shares a supply manifold with two shorter laterals. The pipe lies under a narrow strip of mulch, with a shallow drainage swale about four meters downhill. The ground was soft from irrigation the previous evening, but there had been no rain for six days. Mara shut the row valve and waited for the line to drain before lifting the mulch. Water continued to seep from one point near a connector, although the rest of the exposed pipe remained dry. That detail suggested a local leak rather than a problem at the manifold.

1. The crew isolated the section between the row valve and the final emitter. Luis Ortega used a hand spade to remove mulch and soil in thin layers, taking care not to pull on the nearby emitter tubing. At a depth of about 12 centimeters, he found a split in the 16-millimeter lateral, roughly 30 centimeters from a barbed coupling. The split was on the underside of the pipe and measured about 18 millimeters. The coupling did not appear cracked, and its barb remained seated. Luis said, “The fitting looks sound; the pipe has opened beside it.” Mara photographed the pipe before cutting it, with a ruler and the row marker visible in the frame.

2. The damaged part was cut out with clean shears. The crew checked the cut ends for flattening and dirt, then trimmed a few millimeters from one end to get a round, clean opening. They used a straight 16-millimeter repair sleeve from the orchard’s parts cabinet and pushed each pipe end fully over the sleeve barbs. The sleeve fit tightly without a clamp. Mara marked the insertion depth with a pencil before joining the pieces, which let her confirm that neither end had shifted while the crew handled the pipe. The repaired length remained aligned with the existing lateral and did not rest against the coupling or a tree stake.

3. Before covering the repair, Mara reopened the row valve slowly. She watched the connection for several minutes while Luis checked the emitter at the end of the line and compared its flow with an emitter on the neighboring row. No water appeared at the cut, and the far-end pressure reading returned close to the measurement from the previous week. The emitter flow looked similar by eye, but the crew did not have a flow meter with them. Mara noted that limitation in the work log rather than recording a measured flow rate. They left the repair exposed during the rest of the test so any new seepage would be easy to see.

4. The soil around the line was still damp, so the crew placed the excavated soil on a tarp instead of piling it against the pipe. They removed two small stones from the trench and checked that the drainage path remained open. The mulch went back only after the repair area stayed dry through a second short test. Luis spread it evenly without pressing it onto the lateral. The orange flags remained in place, and Mara added a small map mark showing the repair’s distance from the row marker. The crew took the tarp and cut pipe back to the equipment shed for disposal and inventory.

The work log includes the date, block, row, pipe size, approximate split length, parts used, and the two pressure readings. Mara attached the before-and-after photographs and noted that the leak was found on the underside of the lateral near the barbed coupling. She also recorded that the screen had leaf grit but was not blocked, since that observation may help if pressure falls again elsewhere in the block. The filter was returned to its housing after inspection, and the main valve remained in its normal operating position. The row valve was left open for scheduled irrigation.

The repair sits in a section where equipment access is limited by the swale and by a line of established pear trees. The tractor cannot pass between the rows when the ground is soft, so the crew brought the spade, shears, sleeve, tarp, and pressure gauge by hand. A shallow rut beside the lower access path had collected water earlier in the season, but it was dry during this visit. Mara asked the crew not to widen the excavation unless the sleeve moved or the leak returned. That kept the disturbed area small and left the nearby feeder roots covered.

During the test, Luis heard a brief hiss from the manifold, then saw that it came from water leaving an air-release point as the line refilled. The sound stopped after the pressure settled. He checked the manifold’s unions and the two neighboring row valves; neither had visible moisture. Mara entered the hiss in her notes because it occurred during the refill, but she did not list it as a leak. If pressure drops again while the filter remains clear, the crew will compare the far-end reading on row 18 with the neighboring rows before opening the repaired section. That condition matters because the shared manifold can affect more than one lateral.

The final inspection covered the pipe alignment, sleeve position, mulch depth, nearby emitters, and the drainage swale. The lateral was not under tension, and the repaired segment had enough room to move slightly with changes in temperature. The two flags and map mark identify the location for a later check without relying on the photographs alone. Mara left the work log in the irrigation shed with the gauge readings and parts count, while the images remained attached to the orchard’s maintenance record.
